After a year of questions, the market is pricing Netflix like a franchise whose growth is running out. What we see is a business still growing revenue at double digits, widening its margins and buying back stock at a record pace.

Sentiment and fundamentals have drifted apart, and that is why our model remains constructive even after expectations were revised hard.

A 45.92% Slide That Ignored an Earnings Beat

Netflix is down 4.87% over the past week, 8.49% over the past month, 5.09% over the past quarter and 28.4% year to date. The stock has lost 45.92% over one year. The shares are 42.5% below their 52-week high of $116.73 and just 4.7% above the $64.10 low.

Third-quarter results on October 20 show how wide that gap has become. EPS of $0.87 beat the $0.8229 estimate. Revenue of $12.874B (+11.85% YoY) came in just short of the $12.878B consensus. Operating margin widened to 34.6% from 28.2%.

Why Bulls See $112.90 Ahead

The bull case hits $112.90. Advertising is still early. Management said, "We are still growing our ads business over 80% this year," and ad tiers launch in 15 new countries starting March 2027. Pricing power looks solid, with Q3 churn better than forecast both globally and in the U.S. LatAm revenue rose 17%.

Netflix bought back 63.9M shares for $4.8B in Q3 and has $22.3B left on its authorization. Analysts agree, with 7 Strong Buy and 28 Buy ratings against 15 Hold and 1 Sell.

The FCF cut comes from a one-time Q4 real estate transaction. The margin guidance factors in roughly 120 bps from job cuts that should lower costs over time.

Netflix Earns Its Premium Over Disney and Spotify

Disney (NYSE:DIS) competes directly for streaming subscribers. It trades at 16x earnings, but its operating margin is 14.6%, about half of Netflix's 29.49%.

Spotify (NYSE:SPOT) runs the same subscription-plus-ads model. Its Q3 revenue rose 16.32%, yet it trades at 49x earnings. Netflix sits between the two with the best margins, which makes our 24/7 Wall St. price target look reasonable and arguably conservative.

title: Spotify Is “Highly Defensible” Against AI, Says Jefferies. Its October 22 Report Has to Prove It

Spotify Is “Highly Defensible” Against AI, Says Jefferies. Its October 22 Report Has to Prove It

Spotify Is "Highly Defensible" Against AI, Says Jefferies. Its October 22 Report Has to Prove It ©inkdrop, Bongkarngraphic from bongkarngraphic via Canva
Key Takeaways

Jefferies raised its Spotify price target to $620 from $600 and called the platform highly defensible against AI, while the stock is down 8.5% in 2026.

Margins are the best test of that call, because a business losing ground to AI shouldn't be able to keep raising prices and keep more of every euro.

Spotify guided to a 32.9% gross margin and €670 million of operating income for the third quarter, after 33.4% and €655 million in the second.

At about 35x forward earnings, the stock gets cheaper quickly if margins keep climbing, though a soft subscriber count or Q4 outlook could still overshadow a strong margin print.

Spotify (SPOT:NYSE) stock is down 8.5% in 2026 (through Tuesday's close), as investors worry about what AI could do to a subscription music business.

Jefferies thinks the market has it wrong, and Spotify gets its chance to show which side is right when it reports third-quarter results before the open on Thursday, Oct. 22.

What Jefferies is betting on

On Tuesday, Jefferies kept its Buy rating and raised its price target to $620 from $600, about 18% above Tuesday's close. Analyst James Heaney called Spotify's platform "highly defensible against AI disintermediation fears."

His reasons: expectations are muted, he expects operating expense growth to peak this quarter, and he sees advertising improving as programmatic sales become a bigger part of the business. (Ads could use the help: ad-supported revenue grew just 1% in the second quarter.) He also expects price increases in the US and UK within the next six to 12 months.

Then there's the AI angle. Jefferies sees a possible launch announcement later this year for an AI-powered remixing product tied to Spotify's partnership with Warner Music Group. But its base case includes no AI revenue at all, so none of that $620 depends on AI paying off.

TIKR tracks 40 analysts on Spotify. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Spotify, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Spotify's Analyst Ratings

Pricing power shows up in margins

If AI were really pulling listeners away from Spotify, pricing is where you'd see it first. People who have somewhere better to go don't keep paying more.

Spotify's subscribers keep paying more. In the second quarter, Premium revenue grew 15% to €4.33 billion, from 9% more subscribers and 7% higher revenue per user.

Those price increases have widened the gross margin, from 25.0% in 2022 to 32.0% in 2025…

The most talked about and market moving research calls around Wall Street are now in one place. Here are today's research calls that investors need to know, as compiled by The Fly.

Top 5 Upgrades:

Barclays upgraded Tesla (TSLA) to Overweight from Equal Weight with a price target of $450, up from $370. The firm cites Tesla's merger opportunity with SpaceX (SPCX), stronger core business outlook, and signs of Robotaxi inflection for the upgrade.

UBS upgraded Ross Stores (ROST) to Buy from Neutral with a price target of $315, up from $239. The firm believes the company's store sales growth momentum can persist beyond this year.

Morgan Stanley upgraded Lockheed Martin (LMT) to Overweight from Equal Weight with a price target of $835, up from $690. Top 5 Downgrades:

Morgan Stanley downgraded Block (XYZ) to Equal Weight from Overweight with a price target of $80, down from $90. The company's "bullish expectations" create modestly higher risk to near-term growth and profitability expectations, the firm tells investors in a research note.

Phillip Securities downgraded Spotify (SPOT) to Accumulate from Buy with an unchanged price target of $650. The firm cites valuation for the downgrade following the stock's recent rally for the downgrade.

Treasury Bonds:

After one of the wildest weeks in the U.S. Treasury market in years, normalcy returned on Friday, and so did the sellers, as yields rose across the curve. Despite last week's safe-haven buying, the same issues remain, chief among them inflation; with strong manufacturing output and historically low jobless claims, the path is clear for another 25-basis-point hike. It likely will not come at this week's meetings, but it will probably come before year-end. The 30-year bond closed the session at 5.33%, while the benchmark 10-year note was last seen at 5%.

Oil and Gas

The energy complex keeps the inflation narrative alive, and it rose again Friday, as the threat of increased military activity pushed both benchmarks near 6-month highs. When the dust settled, Brent Crude closed at $116, up 3.05%, while West Texas Intermediate finished the day at $103, higher by 3.74%. Natural gas continued its surprising slide, closing lower by 6.01% to finish Friday's trading at $2.63.

Gold:

Precious metals continued their surprising slide on Friday, though they finished the day well off the lows. Instead of being the haven many investors expect, gold has been battered and closed Friday at $3,993, down 0.76%, while silver ended at $53.74, down 1.34%. Gold falling below $4,000 for the first time since July has baffled many retail investors, given weakness in other assets; top analysts say unique margin mechanics and structural shifts in interest rate expectations have driven gold's sell-off.

When big tech and chip stocks got absolutely wrecked last week, it put heavy pressure on institutional funds. When these highly leveraged portfolios take massive losses, managers are forced to dump gold aggressively, since it's so liquid, to scramble for cash and meet margin calls.

title: Got $5,000? 3 Growth Stocks to Buy and Hold Through 2030.
detail:
Got $5,000? 3 Growth Stocks to Buy and Hold Through 2030.
John Ballard, The Motley Fool

NVDA
SPOT
NOW
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If you have some extra cash that you won't need for several years, putting it into growth stocks with durable competitive advantages could pay off. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) leads in AI computing, Spotify Technology (NYSE: SPOT) in audio streaming, and ServiceNow (NYSE: NOW) in software that runs companies' daily operations. Better yet, all three trade at discounts to their typical valuations. Here's why they're worth buying now.

Nvidia

Nvidia designs the chips and computing systems that power artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. Management expects AI infrastructure spending to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion a year by the end of the decade. That's industrywide spending, not Nvidia's revenue, but Nvidia can capture a large share of it.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The stock is up about 18% over the past year, slightly ahead of the S&P 500's 13%, as revenue doubled year over year to about $96 billion in the quarter ending July 26, 2026. Management expects revenue to grow about 70% next fiscal year.

That outlook reflects a chip industry experiencing component shortages, including for memory chips. Nvidia's advantage is that it sees both ends of the AI supply chain. At the September Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology conference, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang explained that Nvidia's size and decades-long relationships with trusted suppliers help it lock in what it needs. On the other end, it sells through the big cloud providers, server makers like Dell, newer AI cloud companies, and governments building their own AI.

That reach lets Nvidia track where new data centers are being built and powered around the world, giving it an early read on demand. It also gives Nvidia many paths to customers beyond a handful of tech giants. Nvidia said its non-hyperscaler revenue grew 138% year over year last quarter to $40 billion, almost as large as the $48 billion in revenue from hyperscalers like Microsoft.

Nvidia stock trades at about 23 times this year's consensus earnings estimate -- well below its three-year average of about 32. For a company that analysts expect to grow earnings at a 50% annualized rate, that's a solid value.

Image source: Getty Images.
Spotify Technology

Spotify's music, podcast, and audiobook service reaches 788 million monthly users, including 306 million paying subscribers. Its 2030 targets call for mid-teens annual revenue growth and an operating margin above 20%, up from 13.5% in the third quarter.

At the September Goldman Sachs conference, co-CEO Gustav Söderström said the longer Spotify operates in a country, the more listeners pay. In Sweden, about half the population pays, and conversion has trended up in other regions. Yet only 3% to 4% of the world pays for a Spotify subscription. Management aims to reach 1 billion monthly users by 2030 and, eventually, 1 billion subscribers.

The stock is down about 15% over the past year after higher spending on AI features and marketing weighed on profit forecasts. Some also fear AI music will lure listeners away, but a recent deal with Universal Music mitigates this risk. The deal allows Spotify to launch AI cover tools for fan-made remixes of their favorite songs, which adds another incentive for users to sign up for a premium subscription.

Spotify stock trades at about 42 times forward earnings estimates, below its three-year average of about 55. That's not too expensive for a company that analysts expect to grow earnings at an annualized rate of 28% over the next several years. That should support superior returns.

ServiceNow

ServiceNow's cloud software helps large organizations run IT help desks and customer service. At its May 2026 investor day, management laid out a base case of over $30 billion in subscription revenue by 2030, roughly double this year's expected total. It's on schedule, with subscription revenue up about 25% year over year in the June-ending quarter.

The stock is down about 17% over the past year amid worries that AI agents will lead to fewer paid employee "seats," or licensed users at businesses. But management said that half of its new business comes from pricing not tied to seats, suggesting the concerns are overblown.

Looking long-term, the main reason to buy the stock is ServiceNow's entrenched position in customers' operations. At the Goldman Sachs conference in September, CEO Bill McDermott said ServiceNow has spent more than 20 years building a contextual map of what goes on inside a company and now runs over 100 billion workflows. Companies that tried building their own AI tools found they cost five to 10 times more than using ServiceNow.

At about 38 times forward earnings estimates, ServiceNow stock trades well below its three-year average of about 48. With analysts expecting about 24% annual earnings growth over the next several years, the stock could outperform the market from here through 2030.

Spotify Technology (NYSE:SPOT) not only saw its third-quarter headline net income fall, but it also whiffed on the consensus analyst estimate. Given that, you'd imagine that investors would have reacted by aggressively selling the music streamer's stock. Well, you'd be very wrong.

The opposite occurred on Thursday after the company published its earnings release -- market players couldn't wait to buy its stock, and it handily beat the S&P 500 index, rising nearly 4%. On Friday, it ticked higher. Let's look at the company's numbers and tease out why it scored such a big win from an ostensibly losing quarter.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Music to their ears

Spotify's quarter was headed by a revenue line that hit almost 5 billion euros ($5.6 billion), for robust year-over-year growth of 16%. By far the bulk of the company's top line comes from its premium services; the take from these rose by 17% to nearly 4.5 billion euros ($5 billion). The remainder came from ad-supported offerings, which collectively rose 10% to 482 million euros ($540 million).

Spotify also managed to grow both its total user base and the crucial segment of that population, premium-service subscribers. The company's total monthly active user (MAU) count rose 11% to 788 million, while the premium subscriber tally increased 9% to 306 million.

Attributable net income, however, went in the opposite direction. It fell to 518 million euros ($580 million) from the year-ago profit of 899 million euros ($1 billion). On a per-share basis, the former result was 2.48 euros ($2.78).

While that revenue number was essentially in line with the consensus analyst estimate, Spotify fell short on profitability. Analysts tracking the stock were modeling net income of 2.84 euros ($3.18) for the quarter.

That bottom-line swoon looked ugly on paper, but it wasn't as grim as it appeared. In the third quarter of 2025, the company benefited enormously from significant finance income derived from share, bond, and warrant valuations, which affected the accounting. It also recorded a 72 million euro ($81 million) tax benefit during that period.

Spotify watchers are aware that these items distorted the 2025 frame's profitability, so the year-over-year drop wasn't particularly concerning to them. They were also impressed that the company topped its guidance for operating income, which came in at 672 million euros ($753 million), and notched a new record for gross margin at 33%. And for a stock increasingly evaluated on free cash flow (FCF), the 735 million euros ($823 million) in FCF it generated during the quarter was heartening.

Streaming forward

Spotify has an enviably high number of growth opportunities. Management ticked off several major ones, including a major expansion of its relatively recent audiobook business, from the current 22 countries to over 180. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence (AI) is at a relatively early stage of deployment for the company; it plans to harness it to offer subscribers more and increasingly varied custom services -- AI playlists, anyone? -- to enhance the listening and music-curating experiences.

It's confident that this will keep those subscriber and fundamental numbers rising. It proffered guidance for its current (fourth) quarter of 818 million MAUs, which, if achieved, would be nearly 9% higher than in the same period of 2025. It's also counting on a sub-9% increase in premium subscribers (to 316 million). As for key financials, management is expecting another pop in revenue, by almost 15% to 5.2 billion euros ($5.8 billion). Operating income is projected to surge 17% to 820 million euros ($919 million). It did not provide a net income forecast.

I feel that, if anything, Mr. Market's reaction to Spotify's third quarter was muted and conservative. The company has established itself as the clear king of streaming music and, increasingly, other aural entertainment options like audiobooks. I feel it's building quite the imposing moat, which more than justifies the valuations that likely moderated investors' reaction to the earnings release (its forward P/E is approaching 52). Yet this company is becoming ever more powerful, and it clearly aims to tap into the numerous, high-potential growth opportunities before it. I'd be a buyer of this stock, even at its seemingly lofty level.

What Happened?

Analysts raised their Spotify Technology (SPOT:NYSE) price targets on October 22 and 23, yet three of the new targets still sit below the stock's closing price. Shares jumped 11.10% to $583.66 on October 22 after a third-quarter report that beat subscriber guidance and forecast fourth-quarter profit above estimates, on a day the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.6%. The move took the stock from about 9.5% below its 2025 year-end close of $580.71 to about 0.5% above it.

Three New Targets Already Trail the Stock

Benzinga's October 23 roundup lists three changes: Cantor Fitzgerald to $550 from $490 and Rosenblatt to $576 from $527, both Neutral, and Guggenheim to $650 from $575 with a Buy. Cantor had cut its target to $490 from $530 on October 12, per TipRanks. Pivotal Research moved to $460 from $420 with a Hold, about 21% below the close, per TipRanks, which also reported Barclays at $650 and Wells Fargo at $660. Raymond James went to $625, per StreetInsider.

Whatever moved those targets, it was not a bigger revenue forecast. TIKR's consensus for fiscal 2027 revenue rose only 0.31% between September 30 and October 23, to about €22.4 billion, while fiscal 2026 slipped 0.13%.

Spotify Analyst Estimates Trend – Revenue (TIKR)

TIKR's Street mean stood at $611.77 on October 22, about $28 above the close, within a range of $459.79 to $720.89. The rating mix shifted between September 30 and October 22, from 24 Buys, 8 Outperforms and 7 Holds to 22 Buys, 9 Outperforms and 9 Holds. The quarter itself missed on two lines: revenue by 0.2%, and GAAP earnings per share of €2.48 against €2.81, a gap TIKR's earnings-day coverage traced to items below operating income.

Spotify Street Targets (TIKR)
Spotify's Co-CEO Bets It Will Be the Last Subscription Users Cancel

Analyst Rich Greenfield asked on the call whether AI agents that compare prices and cancel unused subscriptions could turn Spotify into an interchangeable back-end pipe. Co-CEO Gustav Söderström answered that Spotify has run in the background of Google Maps and Waze for years and grew through it, because the business earns money even when its app is not on screen.

He said more than 100 million users use Spotify roughly 28 days a month, then added: "It's a bold bet but I think on that list of things that you unsubscribe from, Spotify is going to be the last thing that you unsubscribe from." That is a management prediction, not churn data, but heavy daily use is what an agent hunting for forgotten subscriptions would spare.

Spotify Technology SPOT shares climbed 11% on Thursday after the music-streaming giant reported third-quarter results, highlighted by steady subscriber growth, record gross margins and an increasing focus on artificial intelligence (AI).

Revenue Growth and Record Gross Margin

Spotify reported revenue of nearly €5 billion (about $5.6 billion), broadly in line with market expectations. Premium subscription revenue grew 17% year over year, while ad-supported revenue increased 10%.

Spotify came out with quarterly earnings of $2.85 per share, missing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $3.1 per share while it fell from the year-ago level of $3.83 per share. Spotify posted revenues of $5.72 billion in September 2026, surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $5.70 billion.

However, gross margin reached a record 33%, slightly exceeding Wall Street's estimate of 32.9%. The stock surged 11% during Thursday's trading session. SPOT is now up by only 1.5% for the year 2026.

Subscriber Growth Remains Strong

Spotify continued to expand its user base, with monthly active users rising 11% year over year to 788 million. The company expects monthly active users to reach 818 million in the fourth quarter, while revenue is projected to grow about 15%.

AI Becomes a Bigger Part of Spotify's Strategy

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping Spotify's efforts to improve user engagement and personalization. During the quarter, the company introduced a taste profile feature for U.S. premium subscribers, offering insights into their musical preferences. It also integrated its service with Meta's Muse (read: Should You Tap Meta ETFs on Muse's Success or Wait on the Sidelines?).

However, investors questioned whether AI assistants could weaken Spotify's direct relationship with customers by comparing prices, services and usage across platforms.

Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström dismissed these concerns, drawing a parallel with Spotify's existing integrations with Google Maps and Waze. He noted that users have accessed Spotify through these services during their commutes for years without undermining its business model, as mentioned on Yahoo Finance.

Upbeat Outlook

Spotify guided for €820 million of fourth-quarter operating income. The company's fourth-quarter guidance is expected to be 33.8%, up from 33.1% a year earlier.

For the fourth quarter, Spotify expects 316 million subscribers and €5.2 billion of revenue. The revenue figure is a bit below the €5.24 billion analysts expected, according to Bloomberg's consensus, but the subscriber target is above it, per Tikr, as reported by Yahoo Finance.

Management also expects operating-expense growth to moderate, with that moderation continuing into 2027.

Spotify's Premium Valuation

Shares are trading at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 38.45X, compared with 20.59X for the underlying Internet – Software industry. Its price-to-book and price-to-sales ratios are also elevated at 11.09X and 5.12X, respectively, compared with industry averages of 3.36X and 3.10X.

Price Target

Before the earnings release, Spotify's average price target stood at $603.66, based on short-term forecasts from 32 analysts. The targets ranged from $420 to $720. Spotify shares closed at $583.66 on Oct. 22, 2026.

ETFs in Focus

Spotify delivered mixed Q3 results, with strong subscriber growth and solid gross margins offset by an earnings miss. However, its AI-driven personalization strategy and improving profitability outlook could support future growth, making ETFs with SPOT exposure worth watching for investors seeking an entry point through a basket approach.

Spotify-heavy ETFs include the iShares MSCI Sweden ETF EWD, First Trust Dow Jones International Internet ETF FDNI and Global X Social Media ETF SOCL.
